title: The optative

objectives.can: Recognise an optative by its οι, αι or ειη and say what it expresses.

explanation.summary: The optative is the mood of wishes and of what might be. It is rare in the New Testament, with 68 forms in the analysed text, but it is common in classical Greek and in later authors, and it is easy to recognise by the vowel-and-iota sign οι, αι or ει before the ending.

sections.heading: A rare mood that you will still meet
body: In the New Testament the optative has almost died out. In the corpus used here there are 68 optative forms in all. They are found chiefly in two places: in Paul's letters, as wishes and in the formula μὴ γένοιτο, which is frequent in Romans; and in Luke and Acts, where many are in indirect questions. The other writers of the New Testament use it hardly at all.

It is nevertheless worth learning. Classical Greek, which is read by anyone who goes on to Plato or Xenophon, uses the optative in many ways, and later writers who wrote in an older style, including church writers such as Athanasius, use it freely. The library's texts of the Fathers hold many optatives. Learning to recognise the mood now spares you a surprise there.

sections.heading: How to recognise it
body: The mark of the optative is a diphthong ending in iota, put between the stem and the personal ending: οι in the present and in the second aorist (ἔχοι, λάβοι, θέλοι), αι in the first aorist (ἁγιάσαι, κατευθύναι), and ει in the aorist passive and in εἰμί (τηρηθείη, εἴη). Other endings follow: -ν or -μι in the first person singular (δυναίμην, Εὐξαίμην, ὀναίμην are the middle forms), -ς in the second person, nothing in the third singular, -μεν, -τε and -εν in the plural. In the aorist middle the third singular ends in -το: γένοιτο, βούλοιτο.

The first aorist optative has no augment, like all moods other than the indicative. The third singular ends in -σαι, and here a trap awaits: the same letters are also the ending of the aorist active infinitive. Is κατευθύναι an infinitive or an optative? Only the sentence tells. In 1 Thessalonians 3:11 it has the subject ὁ θεὸς … καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν and no other verb, and so it is an optative: 'may he direct'. An infinitive would not normally be the only verb of a clause whose subject stands in the nominative.

The optative has present and aorist forms. As with the other non-indicative moods, they differ in aspect, not in time. Most wishes in the New Testament are aorist, because they name an event as a whole: ἁγιάσαι, πληρώσαι, δῴη.

sections.heading: What the optative expresses
body: A wish, usually in the third person. In 1 Thessalonians 5:23 Paul asks that God make the readers holy: ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς and τηρηθείη. A negative wish uses μή, as in μὴ γένοιτο, often rendered 'by no means!', a strong rejection of a suggestion that has just been made. A wish can also be in the first person: Philemon 1:20 has ἐγώ σου ὀναίμην, 'may I have benefit from you'.

A possibility, with the particle ἄν. Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην; in Acts 8:31 asks how the eunuch could understand, with no one to guide him. Acts 26:29 has Εὐξαίμην ἂν τῷ θεῷ, 'I would pray to God'. The ἄν puts the optative into a clause about what might be, not what is.

An indirect question after a past verb, a characteristic use in Luke and Acts. Luke 1:29: Mary διελογίζετο ποταπὸς εἴη ὁ ἀσπασμὸς οὗτος, 'she was wondering what kind of greeting this might be'. The question, which would be τίς ἐστιν; in direct speech, is reported with an optative because the main verb is in the past. Often ἄν stands with it (τί ἂν εἴη). This follows a rule of older Greek called sequence: after a past main verb, the verb of a subordinate clause may move into the optative.

A remote condition or a hope. Following εἰ, the optative gives a supposition thought of as unlikely or only possible: 1 Peter 3:14, εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε, 'even if you should suffer'. In Acts 17:27 the people were to seek God εἰ ἄρα γε ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὕροιεν, 'if perhaps they might grope for him and find him'.

sections.heading: Reading an optative
body: Do not translate it with 'would' or 'might' every time. Ask three questions. Is the verb the main verb of a sentence, with no ἄν? Then it is probably a wish. Is ἄν there? Then it is a possibility. Does the verb stand in a clause introduced by a question word or εἰ, after a past verb? Then it belongs to an indirect question or a condition. The mood of the verb tells you that the writer or speaker is reporting a thought, not stating a fact.

misunderstandings: Taking a third singular in -σαι for an infinitive. Both end in -σαι. If the sentence has no other finite verb and the subject is named, it is an optative.
Translating every optative as 'might' or 'would'. Most New Testament optatives are wishes ('may…'), and an indirect-question optative is simply a reported question.
Reading μὴ γένοιτο as a prayer or a calm statement. It is the strongest form of rejection, the Greek way of saying 'by no means'.
Treating the optative as a common mood of the New Testament. It is not; it is rare there, and common in the older and the later Greek that you will read afterwards.

deeper.heading: Why it faded
body: The optative was already losing ground in the Greek of the first century. Its work was taken over by the subjunctive, the indicative and the infinitive. Writers who wished to imitate the Attic prose of the fifth and fourth centuries, and some Christian writers of later centuries, brought it back as a mark of style. In this library the text of Athanasius, On the Incarnation, has 61 optative forms, and the Gospel of Mark has one.

deeper.heading: The 'oblique' optative
body: Classical Greek could use the optative for subordinate clauses that report a thought after a past main verb: in indirect statements, purpose clauses and indirect questions. The sequence of moods is a feature of the older language. The indirect questions of Luke and Acts are the nearest survival in the New Testament.

examples.analysis: ἁγιάσαι is an aorist active optative, third person singular, with the sign -αι: 'may he make you holy'. The subject is ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης. τηρηθείη is an aorist passive optative, third person singular, with the sign -θείη: 'may it be kept'. The two wishes stand at the beginning and the end of the sentence, and together they are a prayer for the readers.

examples.analysis: γένοιτο is an aorist middle optative, third person singular, from γίνομαι: the ending -οιτο has the sign -οι-. With μή it forms the fixed phrase μὴ γένοιτο, a strong rejection of the thought that has just been put: 'by no means'. The rest of the verse gives the reason.

examples.analysis: δυναίμην is a present middle optative, first person singular, with ἄν: Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην; 'how could I?'. The optative with ἄν expresses what would be possible. The question is rhetorical: the eunuch cannot understand without a guide.

options: The ending -ειη after -θ-, the optative sign of the aorist passive
The long vowel ω or η
practice.explain: The sign of the aorist passive optative is -θείη, which is built from -θ- plus -ειη. The aorist has no augment outside the indicative, and a long vowel ω or η would point to the subjunctive. The sentence has no verb but this one, and it is a wish: 'may grace and peace be multiplied'.

options: An aorist infinitive, the subject of the sentence
An aorist optative expressing a wish: 'may the God of hope fill you'
check.explain: The sentence has a named subject, ὁ θεός, and no other finite verb. πληρώσαι is therefore the verb, and its ending -σαι here is the optative. Subjunctives need a conjunction or a hortatory first person; an imperative would be πληρωσάτω.

options: 'The Lord rebuked you', a statement about the past
'To rebuke you, the Lord…': an infinitive of purpose
'May the Lord rebuke you': a wish, with the verb before its subject
'Let him rebuke the Lord', with κύριος as object
check.explain: Ἐπιτιμήσαι is an aorist active optative, third person singular. The subject κύριος follows it, and σοι is the dative of the person rebuked. An infinitive would not have a nominative subject, and a past statement would use the indicative.

options: 'I would pray to God': what Paul would wish, a possibility
